evidence: Draft judged: "It’s got to lead somewhere!" It replaces the approved line "And it’s got to lead somewhere!" Compared character for character, the only differences are the leading "And " removed and "It’s" capitalised, which is exactly what the_change says; the curly apostrophe matches the article's own ("Let’s", "It’s"), "It’s got to" is the right contraction, and there is no stray space before the exclamation mark. Meaning: the approved line's content (the state has to lead somewhere; the guide's "A powerful state matters only if something survives it") is untouched; the "And" carried only an additive link to the paragraph above, no content. No claim or fact is added. It occurs once in CONTEXT.txt (line 11) as the section's one-line last paragraph, verbatim. Read cold in context, it follows "So each can correct the other." as the author's closing remark that the co-operation of the modes is not an end in itself. The "It" has an anchor without the "And": the section already uses "It" for the co-operation it is eliciting ("It’s not an electoral process", "It can be peaceful but also precise"), and the earlier "the adult can choose what to do next in the real world" sets up a where-does-this-go thread, so the line is not a new concern from nowhere. The only cost of dropping "And" is that the line stands alone instead of linking onto the paragraph above; the paragraph break and the matching "It" openers cover that. A reader might for a moment bind "It" to "the other" in the line above, but the repeated "It" earlier in the section settles it. Tells: I count T20 as present at section scale only: four paragraphs in a row end on short lines ("Nobody needs to win!", "It can be peaceful but also precise.", "So each can correct the other." and this one), and this is the last of them. I accept it as justified: it is the owner-approved closing line, the change removes a connective and adds no polish or new landing, and it is a blunt exclamation in the section's own register (the section already uses exclamation marks and caps for emphasis), not a quotable antithesis. If anything, dropping a sentence-initial "And" removes a small colloquial connective (T07) rather than adding one. Considered and not counted: T28 (it closes the section on a normative point, but as a demand and not a recap, reassurance or lesson learned, and it is the approved line), T17 (no "X can be Y and still Z" principle), T11 and T06 (it carries the guide's claim, and "somewhere" is colloquial rather than a therapeutic abstraction posing as concrete), T03 (set up as above), T29 (the paragraph is this one sentence). The other rows (T01, T02, T04, T05, T08-T10, T12-T16, T18, T19, T21-T27) and C01-C04 are absent: no first-person stake, scene, filler, negative reveal, colon, tic word, "kid", wrong referent, first-person fact or named-entity claim. Linter: "B7 short landing at paragraph end" accepted, because it is the whole paragraph as the approved line was, it carries the guide's point rather than summing up the paragraph above, and the change only removes "And". "D9 follows the source order" accepted, because a one-line replacement of one line follows its order by construction; T13 and T09 checked, with no slot-filling or equalized weight in the change itself. Note on the writer's ledger: its T14 evidence says the change "puts back the author's own point that Emulate dropped" and its T15 evidence says it "puts back the author's words or meaning"; neither describes this change (Emulate's and-less line, no put-back). Its T20 row is ABSENT because this is the approved line without its "And"; I count the section-scale run as present and justified for that same reason. None of this changes the verdict.
